summary: An informational memo describing how Sun's SKIP protocol lets a Mobile IP node roaming outside its home network negotiate access past a firewall.

eli5.summary: A traveling computer needs a special pass to get past the building guard back home. This describes one way to get that pass.

questions: how does mobile ip work through a firewall
what is the mobile ip traversal extension
why use skip instead of socks for mobile ip
subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IP laptop can negotiate its way past a SKIP firewall into its home network.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP provides no security for data traffic, and a mobile node roaming on the public Internet cannot simply reach its private home network through the firewall.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node wraps its Mobile IP registration and data packets in SKIP headers addressed to the firewall, which authenticates it, relays the packets inward, and sets up a dynamic binding for traffic back; an optional Traversal Extension names firewalls on the path.
tldr.outcome: A roaming node gets a secure channel into its home network. The memo is Informational and leaves open how a node discovers the firewalls on its path.

today: RFC 2356 is an Informational memo from June 1998 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It builds on RFC 2002 for Mobile IP, and its approach is tied to SKIP key management.

sections.title: The Problem, Players and Firewall Limits
sections.content:
The memo specifies what support is needed at the firewall, the Mobile IP home agent and the mobile node so that the node can reach a private network from the Internet. Its example is an employee who attaches a laptop through a dial-up PPP/SLIP account or a LAN, getting a temporary address from IPCP or DHCP that differs from the one used at the office.

The abstract notes that Mobile IP makes no provisions for securing data traffic. The mechanisms here let the node negotiate access past a SKIP firewall and build a secure channel into its home network. They also let it roam into regions that impose ingress filtering or use a different address space. The memo does not address a node that tries to reach its private network while inside another private network.

The cast is a private network behind a firewall (FW), the public Internet, the mobile node (MN) whose permanent address is in the private network, its home agent (HA), an optional foreign agent (FA), and a correspondent node. Without a firewall, Mobile IP works as normally specified, except the node would most likely use a co-located care-of address instead of relying on a foreign agent.

A firewall only passes packets that match a filter or follow an authenticated negotiation. Private addresses add a second obstacle: a packet for an internal address sent from the Internet will probably not be delivered, because Internet routing cannot handle it, which elicits an ICMP host unreachable. So the firewall MUST be explicitly targeted as the destination by outside packets, and the real packet is recovered once it arrives.
sections.eli5: A laptop that travels still wants to use its home office network. This note explains how it can do that safely from anywhere. Mail for a private building must be addressed to its front desk first.

sections.title: Why SKIP Rather Than SOCKS
sections.content:
The memo compares two firewall technologies. SOCKS version 5 needs a TCP session to carry UDP traffic, with a minimum of 4 round trips (6 with GSS-API) before data flows, repeated each time the node registers a new care-of address. It also offers no clear way to encrypt traffic.

SKIP is a sessionless IP security mechanism, so no round trip is needed before the firewall can start relaying: it can do so on the first packet. This assumes SKIP is used with AH so each packet carries authentication, plus ESP encryption. The node and firewall can be preconfigured with each other's authenticated Diffie-Hellman public values or exchange them on the fly. Session-oriented key management schemes need several round trips, which raises the same concern as SOCKS.

SKIP also supports nomadic use. A name space identifier (NSID) and master key identifier (MKID) in the SKIP header tell the receiver which key to use, instead of keying on the IP source address. For example, NSID 1 with the home address as MKID says to ignore the IP source and use the home address. The firewall keeps a nomadic access list entry that allows any source address for a given NSID/MKID, requires an AH header, and records a dynamic binding to the node's current address. The last Registration Request replaces any earlier care-of address, so simultaneous bindings are not supported without a firewall that understands Mobile IP.
sections.eli5: SOCKS makes you go through a long series of questions before you can pass. SKIP lets you show a badge with every packet, so the guard can let you through right away.

sections.title: Channel Choices and Registration
sections.content:
The memo assumes a co-located address and weighs four secure channel configurations. Option I encrypts only between the node and the firewall's outside interface. Option II is end-to-end encryption through the firewall, which security staff are unlikely to accept because the weaker home agent would do the authentication. Option III makes the firewall a party to the security association for intermediate authentication, which means disclosing the pairwise long-term Diffie-Hellman shared secret to it, unsavory to the end user. Option IV encrypts on both the public and private sides. Options I and IV are essentially equivalent, and the rest of the memo assumes option IV, which also protects traffic from eavesdroppers inside the private network.

When outside, the mobile node MUST encapsulate its Registration Request in a SKIP packet destined to the firewall. It must tell inside from outside addresses, and direct user input can help. The packet carries NSID 1 with the node's IPv4 address as Master Key-ID. The firewall decrypts it, uses it to build a dynamic binding between the care-of address and the permanent address, then re-encrypts toward the home agent. The Registration Reply comes back the same way, and must leave through the same firewall that forwarded the request, unless the firewall understands Mobile IP.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to seal the envelope along the trip. The note picks the safest one, which seals it on the open road and again inside the building.

sections.title: The Traversal Extension
sections.content:
Mobile nodes MAY include a Traversal Extension in Registration Requests, and home agents MAY include it in Registration Replies. It is an explicit notice that one or more traversal points, such as firewalls, lie between the node and its home agent. A node SHOULD include one per traversal point, in the exact order packets meet them.

It carries a Type of 129, a Length of 10, a Reserved field of 0, an MN to HA Traversal Address (typically the firewall's external address) and an HA to MN Traversal Address (typically its internal address). Because the type falls in the range 128 to 255, a receiver may silently ignore it, so it is essentially a hint. It does not say how access is negotiated, and the memo does not solve firewall discovery.
sections.eli5: It is a note on the registration saying which guards the packet will meet, listed in order, so each side knows where to aim its mail.

sections.title: Data Transfer
sections.content:
Data follows the registration pattern. A mobile node sending to a correspondent in the private network encrypts to the firewall with the inner packet sourced from its home address, and the firewall decrypts and injects the inner datagram into the private network. If internal routing might not accept that source address, the node can use a bi-directional tunnel with the home agent. Communication with hosts that need other firewalls or proxies when the node is at home MUST use a bi-directional tunnel while on the public network.

In the other direction, the home agent tunnels a correspondent's packet to the care-of address and sends it inside a SKIP packet to the firewall's inside address. The firewall recovers it and, using the dynamic packet filter set up by the Registration Request, encrypts it for the mobile node.
sections.eli5: Outgoing mail goes to the front desk in a sealed envelope, and the desk delivers it inside. Incoming mail is re-sealed by the desk for the traveler.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Letting IP packets flow through a firewall has perils. The mobile host extends the periphery of the private network, so it MUST take on part of the responsibility for securing it, and MUST have some firewall capabilities. Otherwise a malicious person who gains access to it also gains access to the private network. The node may still need to exchange unencrypted packets with public hosts, for example to meet billing requirements or renew a DHCP lease, in which case it might filter on protocol and port numbers as well as source address.
sections.eli5: If the traveling laptop gets taken over, the thief gets a key to the home building. So the laptop has to act like a guard itself.
